titre: The Tower of Pisa owes its survival to a construction site halted for nearly a century
accroche: Around 1178, work on the Tower of Pisa stops. The clay has nearly a century to harden: according to engineer John Burland, without that pause the tower would have fallen.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1990, the Tower of Pisa closes to the public. Engineer John Burland, who worked on its stabilization, writes that its foundations were then about to become unstable. The tower, however, had been standing for more than eight centuries. It owes this less to the strength of its walls than to a pause in construction whose cause remains unknown.

## Foundations laid on soft clay

Construction begins in August 1173. The foundations, 19.6 meters in diameter, go down only 5.5 meters at most, through three very different layers of soil. The most dangerous is a very soft marine clay, which extends to a depth of 40 meters. Under the tower's weight, this clay compresses, and in compressing it hardens: this is consolidation. The tower has thus sunk about 3 meters on average.

Around 1178, construction reaches a quarter of the way up the fourth level and stops. Burland notes that the reason for the halt is not known; the usual explanation is the wars the Republic of Pisa was waging against Genoa, Lucca, and Florence. Work does not resume until around 1272, nearly a century later. In the meantime, the clay has gained strength under the load already placed on it. Had construction continued without interruption, Burland writes, the clay would not have carried the weight and the tower would have fallen. The scenario repeats: the seventh level is reached around 1278, another halt, and the bell chamber is not raised until around 1360-1370, on soil that has consolidated again. Almost two centuries separate the first stone from the last.

## A tilt the builders tried to correct

At the end of the first phase, the tower leans about a quarter of a degree to the north. When work resumes, it tips to the south: 0.6 degrees in 1278, 1.6 degrees in 1360, 5 degrees in a plumb-line measurement in 1817. The masons tried to compensate by placing wedge-cut blocks on each story, which curves the tower's axis: it does not lean in a straight line, it arcs. Burland links the sharp increase in tilt that accompanies the seventh level and the bell chamber to what he calls tilt instability. It is the effect you see when stacking toy bricks on a carpet: you can go up to a critical height, no further, however careful you are. The tower, he writes, was right at that height.

## What the stabilization aimed at

In 1838, architect Alessandro della Gherardesca digs a walkway, the catino, around the base to expose the column bases. On the south side, the excavation goes below the water table, water rushes in, and the tilt increases by more than a quarter of a degree. In the twentieth century, the lean keeps growing every year: in 1990, the top is moving about 1.5 millimeters a year.

The commission appointed that year did not try to straighten the tower. It aimed for a reduction of half a degree, invisible to the eye, enough to stabilize the foundations and ease the stresses in the masonry. In 1993, 600 tonnes of lead are placed on the north side. Then, starting in February 1999, soil is extracted from beneath the north foundation, twenty liters a day at first, about 120 liters a day once extraction is expanded. In June 2001, the tower is returned to the Pisa authorities. It has regained the tilt it had in 1838.

## What the tower shifts

The Tower of Pisa is often reduced to a foundation error. Burland's analysis adds a lesser-known fact: the halts in construction gave the clay time to harden, whereas the 1838 excavation also brought the tower closer to collapse. Its builders knew nothing about the consolidation of clays. What remains is the question Burland leaves open: why, around 1178, did construction stop?

repere.texte: Closed in 1990, the Tower of Pisa was returned to the city authorities in June 2001. Its stabilization reduced its tilt by 1,830 arcseconds, or half a degree, which amounts to a displacement of 440 mm to the north at the seventh level: it is back to the tilt it had in 1838.

carte.punch: The Tower of Pisa stands thanks to a construction site halted for nearly a century.
carte.idee: Around 1178, work on the Tower of Pisa stops. The subsoil clay, which compresses and hardens under load, has nearly a century to gain strength: without that pause, writes John Burland, the tower would have fallen.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: The stabilisation of the Leaning Tower of Pisa, Ingenia
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The full account of the stabilization by the engineer who led it, with the soil extraction trials and the commission's decisions.

quiz.question: Why did the halt in construction around 1178 probably prevent the tower's collapse?
choix: The masons used the pause to reinforce the foundations with wooden piles
The masons replaced the foundation mortar with a stronger mortar
The subsoil clay compressed and hardened under the weight already placed on it, and carried more when work resumed
The architects lightened the design by dropping several stories when work resumed
quiz.explication: Under load, marine clay compresses and gains strength: this is consolidation. Burland writes that without an interruption it would not have carried the weight. No source mentions piles, a new mortar, or a lightened design.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did the builders try to compensate for the tower's tilt during construction?
choix: By placing wedge-cut blocks on each story, which curves the tower's axis
By anchoring the upper stories to cables stretched toward the north
By weighing down the north face with stone fill
By rebuilding each story narrower than the one before
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Wedge-cut blocks were placed on each story to bring the axis back against the lean, hence the tower's arched shape.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the stabilization completed in 2001 aim for?
choix: Straightening the tower to vertical to make it symmetrical again
Reducing the tilt by half a degree, invisible to the eye, to stabilize the foundations
Replacing the medieval foundations with a modern slab
Supporting the tower with visible props on the south side
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The commission aimed for a reduction of half a degree, not visible, enough to stabilize the foundations. Conservation conventions rule out invasive interventions and visible props, which could have triggered the collapse of the fragile masonry.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What caused the tower's tilt to increase by more than a quarter of a degree in 1838?
choix: An earthquake that shook the Arno plain
The weight of new bells installed in the belfry chamber
A flood that saturated the soil under the tower
A walkway dug around the base, below the water table on the south side
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Architect Gherardesca dug the catino around the base; on the south side, the excavation is below the water table and water rushed in, which increased the lean.
